Order 
This petition under Article 227 of the Constitution of India has been preferred by petitioner being aggrieved by the impugned order dated 12.08.2025 passed in Regular Civil Appeal No.70/2025 by Principal District Judge, Gwalior and Appellate Tribunal under Food Safety and Standards Act,
whereby Appellate Court has rejected the application under Section 5 of the Limitation Act preferred by petitioner.
Brief facts of the case are that Food Safety Officer has inspected the petitioner's firm where the petitioner found present and operating the business of firm.
During inspection, the Food Safety Officer found various food articles stored in the shop like Vadapay, Burger, Dabeli which were used for preparing and selling for consumption in the premises.

Those articles are found being sub-standard and misbranded, therefore, the Food Safety Officer took the sample of those articles for its analysis to the Public NEUTRAL CITATION NO. 2025:MPHC-GWL:22492 2 MP-5090-2025 Analyst Bhopal from where the same report was prepared wherein the samples of some articles were found misbranded.
Thereafter, Foot Safety Officer filed one private complaint before the Adjudicating Officer wherein the show cause notice was issued to the petitioner.
Petitioner filed his reply and denied all the allegations.
After taking evidence, cost of Rs.50,000/- was imposed upon the petitioner under Section 52 of the Food Safety and Standards Act vide order dated 25.10.2024.

sentences.text: Thereafter, being aggrieved by the order dated 25.10.2024, petitioner filed an appeal before Food Safety Appellate Tribunal along with an application of condonation of delay.
Appellate Tribunal after hearing counsel for both the parties, rejected the application filed under Section 5 of the Limitation Act.

Being aggrieved by the impugned order of Appellate Tribunal, petitioner filed this petition with submission that impugned order is not in consonance with the spirit of law and only on the ground of limitation the whole appeal ought not to have been dismissed.

Petitioner has shown sufficient reasons in the application under Section 5 of the Limitation Act for condonation of the delay by stating that the copy of the impugned order dated 25.10.2024 has been received by the petitioner on 08.11.2024 and thereafter, petitioner contacted his counsel to prepare the appeal and the same was filed before the Tribunal on 20.01.2025.
Thus, the delay of 13 days is bona fide and inadvertent.
Hence, prayed for setting aside the impugned order passed by Appellate Tribunal.
On the other hand, learned counsel for the State supported the impugned order and prayed for rejection of petition.
NEUTRAL CITATION NO. 2025:MPHC-GWL:22492 3 MP-5090-2025 Heard learned counsel for the parties and perused the documents available on record.

According to Rule 3.3.1 Food Safety and Standards Act:-
Every appeal under Section 70 of the Act arising out of a decision of the Adjudicating Officer appointed under Section 68 of the Act, shall be filed within a period of 30 days from the date on which the copy of the order against which the appeal is filed, is received by the appellant.

Provided, however, that the Appellate Tribunal may allow a maximum of another 30 days to entertain an appeal if it is satisfied that there was sufficient cause for not filing the appeal within first 30 days.

So, on perusal of Rule 3.3.1 of Food Safety and Standards Act, it is clear that appeal must be filed within thirty days and next thirty days must be condoned by the Appellate Tribunal if appellant shows sufficient cause for not filing the appeal on time.
But, in the present case, a copy of the order was received by petitioner on 08.11.2024 and appeal was filed on 20.01.2025, therefore, appeal is barred by 41 days.
So, it is clear that delay is of just 41 days which is normal in nature.

The Apex Court in the case of N.Balakrishnan Vs. M. Krishnamurthy (1998) 7 SCC 123 in Para 10 and 11 has held as under:-

The reason for such a different stance is thus:

sentences.text: The primary function of a court is to adjudicate the dispute between the parties and to advance substantial justice.
The time-limit fixed for approaching the court in different situations is not because on the expiry of such time a bad cause would transform into a good cause.
11. Rules of limitation are not meant to destroy the rights of parties.
They are meant to see that parties do not resort to dilatory tactics, but seek their remedy promptly.
The object of providing a legal remedy is to repair the damage caused by reason of legal injury.
The law of limitation fixes a lifespan for such legal remedy for the redress of the legal NEUTRAL CITATION NO. 2025:MPHC-GWL:22492 4 MP-5090-2025 injury so suffered.
Time is precious and wasted time would never revisit.
During the efflux of time, newer causes would sprout up necessitating newer persons to seek legal remedy by approaching the courts.
So a lifespan must be fixed for each remedy.
Unending period for launching the remedy may lead to unending uncertainty and consequential anarchy.
The law of limitation is thus founded on public policy.
It is enshrined in the maxim interest reipublicae up sit finis litium (it is for the general welfare that a period be put to lititgation).
So, in view of the law laid down by Apex Court in the aforesaid case, it is clear that rule of limitation are not meant to destroy the substantive right of the parties.
The right of filing an appeal in terms of provisions of Act of 2006 is statutory right of the present petitioner.
Even otherwise, the delay was also not inordinate.
Therefore, the Tribunal ought to have resorted to a lenient approach in the present case and ought to have allowed the application for condonation of delay.
Therefore, in the considered opinion of this Court, Appellate Court has committed an error in not condoning the delay which is just 41 days.

Looking to the facts and circumstances of the case, in the interest of justice, the delay assigned by petitioner in filing the appeal before the Appellate Authority is bona fide in nature, therefore, the only delay of 41 days in filing the appeal by the petitioner deserves to be and is hereby condoned.

The impugned order passed by Appellate Authority is set aside and the matter is remanded to the Appellate Authority to decide the appeal afresh on merits in accordance with law after giving opportunities of hearing to both the parties.
Accordingly, petition stands disposed of.
